plan.title: Low Two-Tier Walnut-Style Display Table
plan.summary: A low rectangular display table inspired by the foreground piece in the photo, with a solid-wood top, four square legs, a full apron, and a lower shelf. The dining-height table visible behind it is treated as background, not part of this build.
assumptions: The foreground low table is the intended project; the photo provides no scale, so dimensions are estimated at 1500 mm wide, 550 mm deep, and 430 mm high.
Balanced-budget solid poplar is used for the visible parts, with a medium walnut-colored stain to match the photo. The top and shelf are made as edge-glued panels.
The legs are square, straight 60 mm stock for simple, reliable construction; the reference legs appear slightly tapered.
The tabletop is 30 mm thick and the lower shelf is 25 mm thick. The table is designed for ordinary display and household loads, not for sitting or climbing.
Joinery is intentionally left for the next planning stage. The aprons and shelf-support rails are positioned to meet the legs and tabletop or shelf with no gaps.

parts.name: Tabletop
parts.material: 30 mm edge-glued poplar panel, walnut-colored stain
parts.notes: Top surface is at y=430 mm; underside meets the tops of all four legs and aprons.

parts.name: Square table legs
parts.notes: Vertical square legs; their tops meet the tabletop underside at y=400 mm. The legs extend to the floor.

parts.name: Long aprons
parts.notes: One apron on each long side; ends meet the inner faces of the legs and tops meet the tabletop underside.

parts.name: End aprons
parts.notes: Short aprons fit between the legs and meet the long aprons at their edges.

parts.name: Lower shelf support rails
parts.notes: Rails meet the inner faces of the legs. Their top faces at y=180 mm support the lower shelf.

parts.name: Lower shelf
parts.material: 25 mm edge-glued poplar panel, walnut-colored stain
parts.notes: Shelf underside rests directly on both lower support rails.

consumables.name: Wood glue
consumables.note: For glued panel construction and applicable wood joints.

consumables.name: Walnut-colored wood stain
consumables.note: Apply to visible poplar surfaces to approximate the photo.

consumables.name: Clear protective finish
consumables.note: Suitable clear furniture finish for the tabletop and shelf.

consumables.name: Sandpaper
consumables.qty: A small assortment of 120, 180, and 220 grit
consumables.note: For surface preparation and finish sanding.

joints.drive_from: Fit the frame-side screw into each prepared recess on the exposed P2 leg top before setting the frame onto face-down P1; then drive the tabletop-side screw from inside the inverted frame through the fitting into P1.
joints.note: One fitting at each leg. Use the fitting maker's recess dimensions; keep the 15 mm screws centered and verify they cannot penetrate the 30 mm top. Do not glue. Confirm each fitting pivots freely to allow tabletop movement.

joints.drive_from: Fit the frame-side screws into prepared recesses on each exposed P3 top edge before setting the inverted frame onto face-down P1; then drive tabletop-side screws from inside the inverted frame through the fittings into P1.
joints.note: Two fittings per long apron, spaced evenly. Use the fitting maker's recess dimensions and verify each fitting pivots freely. The 15 mm screws cannot pass through the 30 mm top; do not glue.

joints.drive_from: Fit the frame-side screw into each prepared recess on the exposed P4 top edge before setting the inverted frame onto face-down P1; then drive the tabletop-side screw from inside the inverted frame through the fitting into P1.
joints.note: One centered fitting per end apron. Use the fitting maker's recess dimensions and verify it pivots freely. The 15 mm screws cannot pass through the 30 mm top; do not glue.

joints.drive_from: From the pocket holes in each P3 end, into the face grain of P2.
joints.note: Two screws per contact. Use the pocket-jig maker's setting for 19 mm stock and its matching stop-collar setting; test on matching offcuts before drilling finished parts. Apply wood glue to the mating faces, clamp square, and do not rely on screws into end grain.

joints.drive_from: From the pocket holes in each P5 end, on the rail's inside face, into the face grain of P2.
joints.note: Two screws per contact. Use the pocket-jig maker's setting for 20 mm stock and matching stop-collar setting; test this rail-to-leg configuration on matching offcuts. Apply wood glue to the mating faces and clamp; screws enter leg face grain.

joints.drive_from: Drill the P3 holes from the inside faces and the matching P4 holes into the P4 end grain before assembly; clamp across each corner.
joints.note: At each corner, use two dowels centered vertically in the 100 mm apron height. Drill 13 mm into P3 and 30 mm into P4, giving 3 mm combined glue clearance around the 40 mm dowel; the P3 holes leave 6 mm behind the outside face. Glue dowels and both mating surfaces, then clamp square for at least 45 minutes.

joints.drive_from: With the table inverted and P6 temporarily supported against the rail tops, drive upward from the exposed undersides of P5 through the slots and washers into pilot holes in P6.
joints.note: Four screws and washers per rail. Use 14 mm-long by 5 mm-wide slots, elongated across P6's width; orient P6 grain along its 1300 mm length so slots accommodate cross-grain movement. Center the screws in the slots, pilot-drill P6, use washers that bridge the slots, and leave screws snug but able to slide. No glue.

steps.title: Prepare panels and cut the parts
steps.text: Make P1 (tabletop) and P6 (lower shelf) as edge-glued panels, with P6's grain running along its 1300 mm length. Cut all parts to their listed dimensions and label their orientation. Clamp panel glue-ups for 60 minutes, then leave them undisturbed for the glue maker's full cure time.
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection when sawing, keep hands clear of the blade, and support long stock. Get help handling the large tabletop panel.
steps.tip: Check both diagonals of each panel; equal diagonal measurements help confirm it is square.

steps.title: Sand and mark the components
steps.text: Sand visible surfaces and edges of P1–P6 with 120 grit, then 180 grit. Mark inside faces, the upper edges of P2–P4, and all future glue areas; leave glue areas clean and uncoated. Ease exposed sharp edges lightly without changing the fixed dimensions.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection; use dust extraction or work in a well-ventilated area.
steps.tip: Keep the sanding block flat on edges so they remain square.

steps.title: Prepare all holes, recesses, and slots
steps.text: Use the pocket-hole jig maker's chart and stop-collar settings for 19 mm P3 and 20 mm P5; drill two holes at each P3 and P5 end, and test both configurations on matching offcuts first. At each apron corner, drill two dowel holes in the P3 inside face to 13 mm depth and matching holes into the P4 ends to 30 mm depth; center them vertically at about 30 mm and 70 mm from the apron edges. Following the selected figure-eight fitting instructions, rout recesses and frame-side pilot holes in P2–P4 upper edges; also cut four 14 x 5 mm slots across the width of each P5 rail.
tools_used: Pocket-hole jig and matching stop collar
steps.safety: Clamp parts securely before drilling or routing. Wear eye protection and keep hands clear of bits and cutters.
steps.tip: Mark paired P3/P4 corners and dry-fit the dowels before gluing; the P3 face holes must not break through the outside face.

steps.title: Stain the components
steps.text: Apply walnut-colored stain to visible surfaces of P1–P6, following the product directions. Keep glue surfaces at P2/P3, P2/P5, and P3/P4 bare, and let the stain dry at least 24 hours or as stated on its label. Test the color on an offcut first.
steps.safety: Wear gloves and provide strong ventilation. Spread stain-soaked cloths out to dry safely or dispose of them according to the label; they can self-heat.
steps.tip: Wipe off excess stain consistently so the large top does not develop dark, sticky patches.

steps.title: Dry-fit and square the frame
steps.text: Arrange P2–P5 in their final positions without glue or screws. Match each marked P3/P4 corner and check that the dowels align, the rails sit at the listed shelf height, and the aprons meet cleanly. Measure the frame diagonals and confirm it is square before taking it apart for assembly.
steps.tip: Label every corner during the dry fit so parts return to the same orientation.

steps.title: Attach the long aprons to the legs
steps.text: Apply wood glue to each P2/P3 mating face and clamp the long aprons square against the legs. Drive two 32 mm coarse-thread #8 pocket-hole screws at each contact from the P3 end holes into the P2 face; use eight screws total. Leave clamps on for at least 45 minutes.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while driving screws and keep the work clamped securely.
steps.tip: Do not overtighten; stop when the joint closes firmly and the apron remains flush with the leg.

steps.title: Install the lower shelf support rails
steps.text: Apply wood glue to each P2/P5 contact face and clamp the rails at their marked height. Drive two 32 mm coarse-thread #8 pocket-hole screws at each contact from the rail's inside face into the leg face; use eight screws total. Check that both rails are level and parallel, then clamp for at least 45 minutes.
steps.safety: Support the frame so it cannot tip while you work, and wear eye protection when driving screws.
steps.tip: Measure from the same end and reference edge on both sides to keep the rails aligned.

steps.title: Join the apron corners
steps.text: At each matched corner, apply wood glue to the P3/P4 mating surfaces and two 8 x 40 mm hardwood dowels. Seat the dowels in the 13 mm P3 face holes and 30 mm P4 end holes, then bring the corners together and clamp square for at least 45 minutes. Use eight dowels total and allow the glue to cure overnight before loading the frame.
steps.safety: Keep fingers out of closing joints while clamping, and wipe glue squeeze-out before it hardens.
steps.tip: If a corner will not close with hand pressure, stop and check dowel alignment rather than forcing it.

steps.title: Cure and prepare for tabletop attachment
steps.text: Leave the glued frame undisturbed overnight, then check that it remains square and all joints are secure. Confirm the figure-eight recesses and frame-side pilot holes are clear, and lay P1 face-down on a padded, clean surface. Keep P6 off the frame until the tabletop is attached.
steps.safety: Use a helper to move the large panel and keep the frame stable while checking it.
steps.tip: Protect the stained face of P1 from grit, which can scratch it during assembly.

steps.title: Attach the tabletop with figure-eight fittings
steps.text: With the frame upright and P6 still absent, fit the figure-eight kits into the prepared P2–P4 recesses and drive their included 15 mm frame-side screws; use one at each P2 leg, two along each P3 apron, and one centered on each P4 apron, 10 kits total. Place the frame upside down and centered on face-down P1, then drive the included 15 mm tabletop-side screws through each exposed fitting into P1; do not glue. Check that every fitting pivots freely and that the screws do not penetrate the top.
steps.safety: Use a helper to lift and invert the frame onto P1; keep fingers clear as it is lowered and support it securely while fastening.
steps.tip: Check the overhang on all four sides before driving the tabletop-side screws.

steps.title: Install the lower shelf while the table is inverted
steps.text: Keep the table inverted and support P6 against the P5 rail tops with temporary blocks or a helper so it cannot fall. Pilot-drill P6 through the rail slots, then fit four 10 mm washers and drive four 40 mm pan-head #8 screws through each rail into the shelf; use eight screws and eight washers total. Do not glue, and leave the screws snug enough for P6 to slide across its grain.
steps.safety: Support P6 securely while working under the inverted frame, wear eye protection, and keep the table stable.
steps.tip: Center each screw in its 14 mm slot and ensure each washer bridges the slot.

steps.title: Apply the protective finish
steps.text: Apply clear protective finish to the assembled table according to its label, using thin, even coats. Lightly sand between coats with 220 grit once dry; allow the stated recoat time, commonly 4–6 hours, and let the final coat cure at least 72 hours before placing objects on the table. Avoid coating the floor-contact ends of the legs heavily.
steps.safety: Ventilate well, wear gloves and any label-required respirator, and keep finishes away from flames. Follow the product label for safe handling and disposal of used applicators.
steps.tip: Do not rush the cure; a finish that feels dry can still mark under display objects.

review.summary: The assembly sequence is generally workable, and both solid-wood panels have movement-aware attachments. Revise the narrow lower-rail pocket joints and coordinate the apron-corner drilling before releasing the plan.

issues.problem: P5 has only a 30 mm-high face for two pocket holes at each end. Common full-size two-hole jig patterns need a wider face; crowding two pockets into this rail leaves vulnerable edges and risks splitting when the screws are tightened. Testing the stock-thickness setting alone does not establish a workable two-hole layout.
issues.fix: Increase P5's vertical depth to at least 50 mm while keeping its shelf-supporting top at the specified height, and select a jig-approved two-hole pattern with adequate edge distances. Update the parts, step 3 drilling instructions, and step 7 accordingly. Alternatively, retain the narrow rails but replace J5 with a specifically detailed glued mortise-and-tenon or loose-tenon joint.

issues.problem: The J6 dowel bores and J4 pocket holes occupy the same end regions of P3, but only the dowel positions are specified. Depending on the pocket jig's hole spacing, the dowel bores can intersect a pocket or screw path. Separate tests of the two joints would not reveal this.
issues.fix: Provide one coordinated drilling layout for each P3 end showing both J4 pockets and J6 dowels. Make a complete corner test using the selected jig, dowels, and screws before drilling finished parts, and shift the vertical hole positions as necessary to leave intact wood between the bores and screw paths.

plan.title: Two-Step Wooden Step Stool
plan.summary: A compact, two-step stool with thick hardwood treads and laminated plywood side cheeks, matching the stepped silhouette and contrasting dark sides shown in the photo.
assumptions: Dimensions are estimated from the photo because no target dimensions were provided; this is sized as a compact household step stool.
Use 30 mm thick poplar or oak for the treads, stained medium brown to match the photo.
Make each 30 mm thick side cheek by laminating two 15 mm birch plywood pieces; stain the sides very dark brown or black.
The stool is intended for ordinary household stepping. Use sound, void-free plywood, fully glued laminations, and secure tread-to-cheek connections.
The side cheeks have a stepped outline and provide continuous bearing beneath the tread edges; treads fit between the cheeks.

parts.material: 30 mm poplar or oak, edge-glued panel
parts.notes: Fits between the inner faces of the side cheeks. Bottom bears on the lower cheek ledges; secure through the cheek faces into the tread edges.

joints.drive_from: From the inside face of each P3 cheek before fitting the treads; drive the tread-flange screws upward from below while the stool is inverted, with clear access to each bracket.
joints.note: Use one bracket at each cheek. Put two screws into the cheek face and two into the tread underside per bracket. The ledges carry the vertical load; brackets resist tread movement. Keep the tread-flange slots oriented front-to-back and snug screws without clamping the solid tread rigidly across its grain. Do not glue this joint. The fixed parts list has no back/riser panel or P3-to-P3 contact, so a separate plywood anti-racking back cannot be added without changing the validated parts and contact list.

steps.title: Cut the tread panels and cheek blanks
steps.text: Cut P1 (lower tread) and P2 (upper tread) to their fixed 400 x 250 x 30 mm dimensions. Cut four 15 mm birch-plywood blanks, each 500 x 300 mm, for the two P3 (stepped side cheek) laminations. Keep the cheek blanks square and label the pairs.
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection and a dust mask. Secure the stock and keep hands clear of the blade; unplug the saw before adjustments.
steps.tip: Measure both diagonals of each blank to check that it is square before cutting.

steps.title: Laminate the cheek blanks
steps.text: Spread an even coat of wood glue over one face of each 15 mm plywood pair, then align the edges to make two 30 mm P3 cheeks. Clamp each pair flat at roughly 150 mm intervals and wipe away squeeze-out. Leave clamps on for the glue label's clamp time, typically 30–60 minutes, then allow 24 hours to cure before cutting.
steps.safety: Follow the glue label and provide ventilation; avoid prolonged skin contact.
steps.tip: Use cauls or flat scrap boards under the clamps to prevent dents and keep the laminations flat.

steps.title: Cut and smooth the stepped cheek profiles
steps.text: Trace the fixed stepped outline onto both laminated P3 panels, keeping the profiles mirrored as required for the left and right sides. Cut just outside the lines, then sand to the lines and smooth the edges. Keep the bottom bearing edges flat so the stool sits steadily.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and a dust mask. Clamp the panels securely, keep the jigsaw shoe flat, and keep hands outside the cut path.
steps.tip: Cut the two cheeks together only if they are clamped firmly and the saw can cut through the full thickness safely; otherwise cut and check them separately.

steps.title: Dry-fit the stool
steps.text: Stand the two P3 cheeks parallel with their inside faces 400 mm apart, then set P1 and P2 on their matching ledges. Check that both treads sit flat, are centered, and do not rock. Mark bracket positions on the inside cheek faces and tread undersides without changing the fixed geometry.
steps.tip: Confirm the lower and upper tread locations before drilling; reversing a cheek can put a ledge at the wrong height.

steps.title: Sand and prepare the surfaces
steps.text: Sand the treads and cheek faces progressively with 80, 120, then 180 grit, rounding only sharp exposed edges. Remove dust thoroughly and keep the marked bracket areas visible. Do not sand away the flat tread-bearing ledges.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and a dust mask; connect dust extraction where available.
steps.tip: Keep the sander moving to avoid dips, especially near the edges of the treads.

steps.title: Stain and finish the separate parts
steps.text: Apply dark brown or black stain to P3 and medium-brown stain to P1 and P2, following the product directions. Apply several thin coats of clear protective finish, allowing the label's recoat time between coats and at least 24 hours of cure before assembly. Keep finish off the bracket contact areas where practical.
steps.safety: Work with strong ventilation, wear finish-appropriate gloves, and keep stain-soaked cloths spread out to dry safely or dispose of them as directed on the label.
steps.tip: Test the stain on offcuts first; color can vary between plywood faces and hardwood.

steps.title: Fasten the lower tread
steps.text: With the stool inverted, place P1 (lower tread) on its ledges and position one slotted angle bracket at each P3 cheek. Pre-drill, then drive two #8 x 25 mm screws through each bracket into the cheek face and two upward into the tread underside; use four screws per bracket. Keep the tread-flange slots front-to-back, snug the screws without crushing the wood, and use no glue.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and support the inverted stool securely. Keep the drill straight and fingers clear of the bracket edges.
steps.tip: Check that P1 is fully seated on both ledges before tightening; the bearing ledges, not the screws, carry the stepping load.

steps.title: Fasten the upper tread
steps.text: Keep the stool inverted and place P2 (upper tread) on its ledges. Install one slotted angle bracket at each P3 cheek, pre-drilling and driving two #8 x 25 mm screws into each cheek face and two upward into the tread underside per bracket. Keep the tread-flange slots front-to-back, snug the screws without crushing the wood, and use no glue.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and support the stool securely while drilling upward. Keep the drill clear of the other tread and your hands.
steps.tip: Check that P2 is fully seated and level on both ledges before driving the final screws.

steps.title: Inspect and ready the stool for use
steps.text: Set the stool upright on a flat floor and check that it does not rock, both treads bear evenly, and all brackets are secure. Touch up any finish damage and let the touch-up cure fully before use. Do not use the stool if a cheek is cracked, a tread shifts, or a bracket loosens.
steps.safety: Have another person steady the stool during the first checks; do not climb on it until the finish is cured and the assembly has passed inspection.
steps.tip: Recheck the bracket screws after initial use, but do not overtighten slotted tread screws. The provided fixed parts do not include the requested plywood back/riser; this assembly should not be treated as having that added anti-racking reinforcement.

review.summary: The cutting, lamination, and basic assembly sequence are workable, but the stool needs a defined side-to-side bracing system before being used for stepping. Clarify the movement hardware and remove conflicting fastening instructions.

issues.problem: The only connections tying the two cheeks together are four small angle brackets with short screws. There is no back, riser, or diagonal brace to resist side-to-side racking. Calling these brackets heavy-duty and relying on tread bearing does not establish resistance to the sideways forces produced when someone steps onto the stool off-center.
issues.fix: Add a structural plywood back or riser that ties both P3 cheeks together and prevents lateral racking. Attach it through glued-and-screwed cleats on the plywood cheek faces, rather than relying on screws into plywood edges. Specify its material, fasteners, and installation sequence, and install it before access is obstructed. Keep the solid treads independently attached with movement-compatible hardware.

issues.problem: The movement detail specifies slotted brackets but does not specify screw heads, washers, or tread grain direction. Generic wood screws may have countersunk heads that wedge into the slots instead of allowing movement. Front-to-back slots work as intended only when the tread grain runs across the stool's width.
issues.fix: Specify that P1 and P2 grain runs along their 400 mm length. Specify commercially available brackets with front-to-back slots on the tread flange, plus compatible pan-head screws and flat washers that bridge the slots. Center the screws in the slots at assembly and tighten only enough to retain the tread without locking movement. Update both joints and the hardware list.

issues.problem: The P1 and P2 part notes instruct the builder to secure through the cheek faces into the tread edges, while J1, J2, and steps 7–8 specify underside brackets and no such screws. These are materially different fastening methods, and following both could restrain tread movement and introduce end-grain fastening.
issues.fix: Delete the through-cheek fastening instruction from both tread notes. State that J1 and J2 are the only tread attachments and that no additional screws or glue are to connect the solid treads rigidly to the cheeks.

issues.problem: The instruction to trace the fixed cheek outline assumes a usable template, but the plan supplies only SVG path data. That is not a directly usable shop layout for most builders.
issues.fix: Supply a dimensioned cheek drawing or a printable full-size template with a scale-check mark. Label the floor-bearing edges, tread-bearing surfaces, front, rear, and inside faces.

issues.problem: The plan provides clear-finished stepping surfaces and finished wood floor contacts but no positive traction treatment. A non-slip floor alone does not ensure that footwear will grip the treads or that the stool will grip a smooth floor.
issues.fix: Add securely bonded, finish-compatible non-slip strips to both treads and thin non-slip pads to all floor-bearing areas. Specify installation after the finish has fully cured, and confirm that the pads leave the stool sitting evenly.

plan.title: Classroom Desk and Chair Set
plan.summary: A single student desk and matching chair inspired by the classroom furniture in the photo. The desk and chair have separate welded square-tube frames, plywood panels, and painted red chair seat and back.
assumptions: The photo shows separate student desks and chairs, so this plan is for one desk-and-chair set rather than a tablet-arm chair.
Dimensions are estimated from common classroom furniture proportions: desk top 600 × 450 mm at 750 mm high; chair seat at 445 mm high.
The desk is at the front (z=0–450); the chair sits behind it. The complete set footprint is 600 × 906 mm.
Balanced materials: 20 mm birch plywood for the desk top, 18 mm birch plywood for the chair panels, and 25 mm square steel tube for the desk and chair frames.
The chair seat and back are flat plywood approximations of the molded, rounded shells in the photo; red paint approximates the bright red finish.
Steel frame joints are welded. Plywood panels attach to frame members with suitable machine screws or bolts; fasteners are not included in consumables.
The desk top has a dark wood-look laminate or finish. Use suitable edge treatment on exposed plywood edges.

steps.title: Specify and prepare the steel
steps.text: Before buying steel, have a qualified furniture fabricator confirm the fixed frame and back-support design for the intended user load. Specify weldable, uncoated mild-steel square tube: 25 x 25 x 2mm for P2–P9 and 20 x 20 x 2mm for P10, only if the fabricator approves these wall thicknesses and the fixed geometry. Buy clean, bare stock; do not weld galvanized or unknown-coated tube. Cut to the listed lengths, deburr, and label each piece.
tools_used: Angle grinder with cutting and flap discs
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection, gloves for handling stock, and a suitable respirator. Clamp steel before cutting or grinding and direct sparks away from people and flammables.
steps.tip: If the fabricator cannot approve the fixed back-support geometry and specify its connections, stop rather than improvising a chair back.

steps.title: Make the plywood panels
steps.text: Obtain birch plywood in the listed thicknesses, then cut P1 to 600 x 450mm, P5 to 430 x 370mm, and P11 to 400 x 190mm. Mark the specified corner radii of 12mm on P1 and 30mm on P5 and P11; cut the straight edges with a guided circular saw and the corners with a jigsaw or router template. Sand the cut edges smooth without changing the panel sizes.
tools_used: Jigsaw or router with radius template
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection and a dust mask. Clamp the plywood securely, keep hands clear of the blade, and use the saw manufacturer's guards.
steps.tip: Make a small radius template and trace it consistently so matching corners are smooth and even.

steps.title: Mark and drill mounting holes
steps.text: Mark the six plywood screw locations on each desk rail and chair seat rail. At each location, drill a 5.5mm clearance hole in the panel-contact tube wall and an aligned 14mm access hole in the opposite wall for the pan-head screw and long driver extension. Mark two back-panel rivnut positions on the rear-facing wall of each P9 and one separate seat-bracket rivnut position on its inward-facing wall; drill to the body-hole diameter specified by the selected rivnut manufacturer, and drill matching clearance holes in P11. Drill the anti-tip strap hole in rear P3 and deburr all holes.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and clamp each tube securely. Keep hands clear of the bit; never hold small tube pieces while drilling.
steps.tip: Mark the rear-facing and inward-facing P9 holes separately and verify their bracket/back-panel locations before drilling.

steps.title: Sand and finish the plywood
steps.text: Sand P1, P5, and P11 with 120-grit and then 180-grit paper, easing only the cut edges. Apply red enamel to P5 and P11 and the selected dark wood-look finish to P1. Allow at least 24 hours to dry, or longer if required by the product label.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask while sanding and ventilate well while applying finishes. Keep finishes away from flames and welding sparks.
steps.tip: Seal exposed plywood edges thoroughly; they absorb paint and finish faster than the faces.

steps.title: Dry-fit and square the desk frame
steps.text: Arrange P2, P3, and P4 on a flat welding table in the fixed desk layout. Clamp the frame, check that the legs are parallel, and compare the diagonals. Correct alignment before welding.
steps.safety: Wear safety shoes and use clamps to prevent steel pieces from rolling or shifting.
steps.tip: Equal diagonal measurements are a quick check that the rectangular frame is square.

steps.title: Weld the desk frame
steps.text: Have a qualified welder tack P3 to P2 at all four contacts, P4 to P2 at both contacts, and P3 to P4 at both rail intersections. The fabricator must follow the approved weld sizes, lengths, and procedure for the specified tube and keep the top-contact faces flat. Check the frame for square, complete the approved welds, and let it cool before unclamping.
steps.safety: Use a qualified welder with welding helmet, gloves, flame-resistant clothing, ventilation, and a fire extinguisher. Keep others shielded from arc flash and all plywood and finishes away from sparks.
steps.tip: Alternate weld locations to reduce heat distortion.

steps.title: Dry-fit and square the chair seat frame
steps.text: Arrange P6, P7, and P8 on the flat welding table in the fixed chair layout. Clamp the pieces and check the frame diagonals and the heights of all four upper rail faces. Correct any twist before welding.
steps.safety: Wear safety shoes and use clamps; the frame can tip while it is being positioned.
steps.tip: Keep the upper rail faces in one plane so the plywood seat will not rock.

steps.title: Weld the chair seat frame
steps.text: Have a qualified welder tack P7 and P8 to P6 at each listed contact and tack the four P7-to-P8 corners. Recheck both diagonals, then complete the welds to the fabricator's approved schedule for the specified tube. Let the frame cool before unclamping.
steps.safety: Use qualified welding personnel and full welding PPE, ventilation, and fire precautions. Keep sparks away from plywood and finishes.
steps.tip: Check that the frame stands level and does not rock before fitting the seat.

steps.title: Fabricate the chair back support
steps.text: A qualified furniture fabricator must first approve the fixed P6/P7/P8/P9/P10 geometry for the intended user load and provide a written drawing specifying tube wall thickness, connection details, weld sizes and effective lengths, welding procedure, and any required gussets or extended supports. If the fixed geometry cannot be approved, do not fabricate or use the chair; do not improvise additional parts. Following the approved drawing, weld the P10 brace-to-leg, brace-to-rail, brace-to-side-rail, and P9 upright-to-brace contacts. Check the uprights are parallel and plumb, then complete the specified welds.
tools_used: Qualified fabricator's approved drawing and weld schedule
steps.safety: This is a safety-critical back-support connection. Qualified fabrication, welding PPE, ventilation, and fire precautions are mandatory; do not rely on visual inspection or occupant testing to establish strength.
steps.tip: Keep the approved fabrication drawing with the chair records for later inspection.

steps.title: Clean, coat, and install rivnuts
steps.text: Remove weld spatter and sharp edges, then inspect both frames and coat the bare steel according to the coating label. After the coating has cured, install three M6 rivnuts in each P9: two in the rear-facing wall for P11 and one separate rivnut in the inward-facing wall for the seat bracket. Use the manufacturer's specified hole diameter and grip range for the selected 2mm-wall tube, and check each rivnut is set firmly.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and a suitable respirator when grinding or applying coating. Use ventilation, keep coatings away from heat, and clamp parts securely when setting rivnuts.
steps.tip: Keep coating out of drilled holes and verify all six rivnuts are secure before attaching the seat bracket or back panel.

steps.title: Attach the desk top
steps.text: Set P1 face down on a padded surface and place the desk frame on its underside in the fixed position. Drive three #10 x 19mm pan-head screws through each P3 and P4 rail into P1, using the 5.5mm panel-contact holes and aligned 14mm opposite-wall access holes with a long driver extension. Do not add glue; stop when each screw is snug.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and support the frame while turning the desk upright; use a helper if needed.
steps.tip: The short screw length is intentional; longer screws can pierce the visible top.

steps.title: Attach the chair seat to its rails
steps.text: Place P5 upside down on a padded surface and center the chair frame beneath it. Drive three #10 x 16mm pan-head screws through each P7 and P8 rail into the seat, using the 5.5mm panel-contact holes and aligned 14mm opposite-wall access holes with a long driver extension. Do not glue the plywood to the steel; stop when the heads are snug.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and keep fingers away from the screw points and driver bit.
steps.tip: Center the screws on the narrow tube faces and keep them clear of the plywood edges.

steps.title: Secure the seat to the back uprights
steps.text: Fit one 40 x 40 x 2mm angle bracket at each P5-to-P9 contact. Drive two #10 x 16mm screws per bracket into the seat underside, then install one M6 x 16mm machine screw and washer per bracket into the separate inward-facing rivnut in P9. Tighten securely without crushing the plywood.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and support the chair so it cannot tip while fastening underneath the seat.
steps.tip: Check that the brackets do not interfere with the back panel or the finished seat edges.

steps.title: Bolt on the chair back
steps.text: Hold P11 against the rear faces of P9 and align its two clearance holes with the two rear-facing rivnuts in each upright. From the exposed rear face of P11, install two M6 x 35mm machine screws with washers per upright through the panel into those rivnuts. Start all four bolts loosely, then tighten evenly without crushing the plywood; do not glue the panel to the steel.
steps.safety: Use a helper or clamps to hold the panel securely while starting the bolts.
steps.tip: Starting all four bolts loosely helps align the holes without forcing the panel.

steps.title: Install the desk anti-tip restraint
steps.text: Position the desk near a wall stud and attach one end of the 200N-rated anti-tip strap through the rear P3 rail with the M6 x 35mm bolt, washers, and nyloc nut. Secure the wall end with the 6 x 75mm structural screw into the stud. If no stud is available, use a load-rated anchor suitable for at least 200N.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while drilling and check for electrical wiring and plumbing before drilling the wall.
steps.tip: The strap should prevent tipping without pulling the desk frame out of square.

steps.title: Final inspection and curing
steps.text: Set the desk and chair on a level floor and check that they do not rock. Have the completed chair and its back-support welds assessed by a qualified furniture fabricator before use; do not use it as a test of joint strength. Recheck screws and bolts after the first day and respect the finish maker's full cure time.
steps.safety: Do not use the chair until its fabricator assessment is complete. Keep the desk anti-tip strap attached where tipping could be a hazard.
steps.tip: Do not use either item if a weld is cracked, a fastener is loose, or the frame rocks.

joints.drive_from: From below P1, install each plate with its supplied screws before threading the prepared P2 leg onto the plate’s 3/8-16 machine thread.
joints.note: Use Rockler 10° Angled Leg Mounting Plates, a commercially available system marketed for angled furniture/table legs. Rotate each plate so its tilt points radially outward from the tabletop center; the 10° resultant is close to the specified approximately 9.9° compound splay. The 40 mm leg tops suit the plate’s intended furniture-leg application. This is an apronless side table, not seating: confirm Rockler’s current instructions and suitability for the expected lateral as well as vertical loads before building; do not rely on a vertical-load figure alone. No glue; the bolted connection is removable.

joints.drive_from: From below through P3 into the underside face of P1; drive the two outer screws through the slotted holes and washers.
joints.note: Use a 5 mm screw-shank clearance hole at the center of P3 and two 5.5 mm wide by 12 mm long slots at its ends, with the slots oriented across P1’s grain. Flat washers must bridge the slots; do not countersink. Drill separate 3 mm pilot holes 16 mm deep into P1. Glue only a small patch at the center; snug the outer screws only enough to retain P3 while allowing the washers to slide in the slots.

steps.title: Check the layout and grain
steps.text: Confirm P1 (Round tabletop) is 600 mm across and mark its center on the underside. Mark the four P2 (Splayed tapered round leg) attachment centers at the supplied coordinates, measuring from the tabletop center, and mark each leg’s radial outward direction. Identify P1’s grain direction and mark it on the underside so the P3 slots can run across the grain.
steps.tip: Check all four center marks against a full-size layout before drilling.

steps.title: Cut and smooth the tabletop
steps.text: Cut P1 (Round tabletop) to a 600 mm diameter circle with a circle jig and router, or cut just outside the line with a jigsaw and sand to the line. Ease the sharp edge lightly and sand the faces and rim through 120, 150, and 180 grit. Keep the underside leg marks visible.
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection and a dust mask. Secure the panel, keep hands clear of the blade or bit, and disconnect power before changing a bit or blade.
steps.tip: Make shallow passes with the router to reduce tear-out.

steps.title: Turn the tapered legs
steps.text: Turn four P2 (Splayed tapered round leg) blanks to approximately 533 mm long, 40 mm diameter at the top, and 28 mm at the foot. Leave the foot ends uncut for now; their final level cuts must be indexed to the legs’ installed orientation. If you do not have a lathe, have a turning shop make the legs to these dimensions and leave the foot ends long for fitting.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection and a face shield at the lathe; tie back hair and remove loose clothing and jewelry. Secure each blank, and stop the lathe before measuring or sanding.
steps.tip: Use calipers frequently so the four tapers match.

steps.title: Install the hanger bolts in the legs
steps.text: At the center of each P2 (Splayed tapered round leg) top, drill a 6 mm pilot hole 28 mm deep along the leg’s long axis. Fit a 3/8-16 x 50 mm hanger bolt using two jammed nuts or a hanger-bolt driver; embed its wood-thread end 25 mm, leaving approximately 25 mm of machine thread projecting. Keep the bolt centered and aligned with the leg axis.
tools_used: Two jam nuts and wrench or hanger-bolt driver
steps.safety: Clamp each leg securely before drilling or driving the bolt. Wear eye protection and keep hands clear of the rotating drill and wrench.
steps.tip: Use a depth stop; a hole or bolt that breaks through the 40 mm leg top will weaken the attachment.

steps.title: Drill the cleat movement holes
steps.text: On P3 (Underside stiffening cleat), mark three screw positions along its length: one at the center and one near each end. Drill a 5 mm screw-shank clearance hole at the center and two 5.5 mm wide by 12 mm long slots at the ends, oriented across P1’s grain; do not countersink. Mark the tabletop pilot positions through the cleat after alignment, then drill separate 3 mm pilot holes 16 mm deep into P1.
steps.safety: Clamp P3 securely and wear eye protection while drilling. Keep hands clear of the bit and use a depth stop for the tabletop pilots.
steps.tip: Keep the two slots centered across the cleat width so the washers can travel without catching an edge.

steps.title: Attach the underside cleat
steps.text: Align P3 (Underside stiffening cleat) on P1 (Round tabletop) and apply only a small glue patch at the center. Drive three pan-head #8 x 38 mm wood screws with 12 mm outside-diameter flat washers from below through P3 into P1; put the center screw through the round clearance hole and the outer screws through the slots. Snug the outer screws without crushing the slots or preventing washer movement; clamp for 30 minutes and allow the center glue patch to cure for 24 hours.
steps.safety: Wear eye protection while driving screws, and wipe away excess glue before it cures.
steps.tip: Do not substitute countersunk screws or omit the washers; the outer connections must be able to slide across the grain.

steps.title: Mount the plates and establish leg orientation
steps.text: Turn P1 (Round tabletop) upside down on a stable padded support. At each marked center, attach a Rockler 10° Angled Leg Mounting Plate using its supplied #8 x 16 mm screws, orienting the plate’s tilt radially outward; follow the current manufacturer instructions for screw placement and installation. Thread each prepared P2 (Splayed tapered round leg) onto its plate and tighten fully, then check the outward splay, clearance from P3 (Underside stiffening cleat), and stance on a level surface; mark each leg’s installed rotational orientation before removing it.
steps.safety: Support the inverted tabletop so it cannot shift. Keep fingers clear while tightening, and ask for help if needed to turn or support the assembly.
steps.tip: The final foot cuts depend on the fully tightened leg orientation; label each leg and its matching plate location.

steps.title: Mark and cut the feet level
steps.text: With P1 supported level and the P2 legs fully tightened in their marked positions, transfer a level floor-plane line onto each foot. Remove and label each leg, then cut to the marked plane using a rigid cradle shaped to support the taper and positively clamp the leg against rolling; index the cradle to the orientation marks and secure it to the saw setup. Keep every clamp outside the blade path, and confirm the cut face is level when that leg is returned to its marked plate position.
tools_used: Rigid tapered-leg cradle with positive clamps
steps.safety: Wear eye and hearing protection. Secure the cradle to the saw setup and the leg in the cradle before cutting; keep clamps and hands clear of the blade path. If this fixture cannot be made rigid and secure, have a woodturning shop cut the feet to the marked lines.
steps.tip: Do not rotate a leg in its plate after marking its foot; the cut is indexed to that final tightened orientation.

steps.title: Sand and check the assembled table
steps.text: Sand P1 (Round tabletop), P2 (Splayed tapered round leg), and exposed P3 (Underside stiffening cleat) to 180 grit, keeping sanding light on the edges. Reinstall each leg in its labeled position and orientation, tighten it fully, and check that all feet contact a level surface without rocking. Remove dust before finishing.
steps.safety: Wear a dust mask and eye protection while sanding. Support the table securely so it cannot tip.
steps.tip: If the table rocks, check that each leg is fully seated in its plate before making any further foot adjustments.

steps.title: Apply the clear finish
steps.text: Apply a thin, even coat of clear furniture finish to P1 (Round tabletop), P2 (Splayed tapered round leg), and exposed P3 (Underside stiffening cleat), following the product directions. Let it dry for the label’s stated time, lightly sand with the specified fine abrasive if required, and apply two more thin coats. Allow at least 24 hours after the final coat before light use, or longer if the product label requires it.
steps.safety: Work with strong ventilation, wear gloves and the finish label’s required respiratory protection, and dry or dispose of finish-soaked rags as directed.
steps.tip: Thin coats cure more evenly and are less likely to leave runs around the leg plates.

safety_overview: Wear eye protection for cutting, turning, drilling, and sanding; add hearing protection for loud power tools and a dust mask for wood dust.
Secure workpieces before cutting or drilling, keep hands clear of blades and bits, and disconnect power before changing cutting tools.
At the lathe, use a face shield, secure each blank, and avoid loose clothing, jewelry, or tied-back hair coming near rotating stock.
Use finishes only with good ventilation and follow the label for gloves, respirators, drying, and disposal of finish-soaked rags.
Support the table during assembly and ask for help when lifting or turning it over.

review.summary: The assembly sequence is generally workable, and the cleat attachment allows for wood movement. Resolve the leg-top seating detail before building, and complete the cleat fabrication and layout instructions.

issues.problem: P2 specifies both ends as level, but the angled mounting plates require leg tops prepared to match their inclined seating surfaces—normally square to the leg axis. A horizontal top cut on a splayed leg will not seat fully against that surface. Tightening the hanger bolt against an edge rather than a full bearing face can crush the pine and allow the joint to loosen under lateral loading. Steps 3 and 4 never resolve this conflict.
issues.fix: Specify leg-top cuts that match the selected plate manufacturer's seating requirements, normally square to each leg's axis. Change P2's ends description so only the feet are cut parallel to the floor. In step 7, require full, firm seating of each leg shoulder against its plate, and verify that the hanger bolt does not bottom out before the shoulder seats. Retain the indexed foot-cutting procedure in step 8.

issues.problem: The plan moves directly to drilling P3 without ever instructing the builder to cut the cleat or round its ends. It also specifies elongated slots but lists only drill bits, without explaining how to finish those slots.
issues.fix: Add a cleat-preparation operation before step 5: cut P3 from suitable stock, form and sand its rounded ends, and mark its installed orientation relative to P1's grain. Explain that the slots can be made by drilling overlapping holes in a securely clamped cleat and cleaning them up with a small file; add the file to the tool list. Do not use an ordinary drill bit as a sideways milling cutter.

issues.problem: The instruction says to mark the supplied attachment coordinates by measuring from the tabletop center, but the supplied coordinates use the panel's layout origin. Those are different references, so a builder following the wording can mark the plates incorrectly.
issues.fix: Provide a full-size underside template or explicitly distinguish the supplied coordinate origin from the tabletop center. Give center-relative attachment marks and radial orientation arrows in the build instructions rather than asking the builder to interpret the placement data.
